What Is Ad Fraud? Bots, MFA Sites, and Controls

Distribution

In short: Ad fraud is any scheme that generates fake advertising activity so someone is paid for attention that never happened, and it hides inside good-looking reports. Buy through inclusion lists with pre-bid verification, validate outcomes in your own systems, watch for numbers that are too clean, and use partners not paid more when volume rises.

Key points

  • Main forms: invalid traffic, made-for-advertising sites, domain and app spoofing, ad stacking, click and install fraud, and lead and affiliate fraud.
  • The number that matters is the share of your own buy that verification rejected; if you lack it, assume it is not small.
  • Optimise toward outcomes further down the funnel, because fraud is cheapest at the top.
  • Watch for tells: conversion rates too good, unexpected geographies, unusual hours, and a cheap channel that suddenly scales.
  • Intermediaries paid on volume have a reduced incentive to reject volume; flat-fee partners are better aligned.

Ad fraud is any scheme that generates fake advertising activity, impressions, clicks, installs, views, leads, so that someone is paid for attention that never happened. It is one of the largest forms of online crime by value, and most of it is paid for by advertisers who never see it because their reports show it as performance.

The main forms

Invalid traffic. Bots and automated scripts that load pages, view ads, and click. Ranges from crude data-center traffic, easily filtered, to sophisticated bots on hijacked residential devices that mimic human behavior.

Made-for-advertising sites. Pages that exist only to host ads, filled with cheap or scraped content and visited by traffic the site owner bought from arbitrage sources. Technically the visitors may be human; the site has no audience anyone wanted to reach. Industry studies have found a substantial share of programmatic impressions landing on such pages.

Domain and app spoofing. Low-quality inventory misrepresented in the auction as a premium publisher or app, so the buyer pays a premium price for junk.

Ad stacking and pixel stuffing. Many ads layered in one slot, or an ad rendered in a one-pixel frame, so impressions are counted that nobody could have seen.

Click and install fraud. Fake clicks, click injection on mobile devices that claims credit for organic installs, and install farms of real devices operated to collect cost-per-install payments.

Lead and affiliate fraud. Fabricated form submissions, stolen identities used to create accounts, cookie stuffing that drops an affiliate's tracking on visitors who never clicked, and coupon-code abuse.

How large the problem is

Estimates vary by method and vary widely; the industry bodies that measure it put global losses in the tens of billions of dollars annually, with the share of a given advertiser's budget lost ranging from low single digits on well-controlled buys to a large fraction on open-exchange buys with no verification. The number that matters is not the global one. It is the share of your own buy that verification rejected, and if you do not have that figure, assume it is not small.

How it is detected

Third-party verification vendors accredited by industry bodies measure invalid traffic, viewability, and placement quality, pre-bid where possible and post-bid otherwise. Platforms filter the crude forms themselves and report "invalid" activity they caught; they are less forthcoming about what they missed. Affiliate networks apply validation periods and fraud scoring to conversions. The company's own analytics, compared with partner reports, is the final check: outcomes a partner claims that the company's systems cannot see are the signal.

The practical controls

Buy through inclusion lists, not blocklists. Require pre-bid verification on every programmatic buy and read the rejection report. Optimize toward outcomes further down the funnel than clicks or installs; fraud is cheapest at the top. Validate every paid outcome in your own systems before paying for it, with a delay long enough to catch reversals. Watch for the tells: conversion rates too good, traffic from unexpected geographies, activity at unusual hours, a partner whose numbers never fluctuate. Cap any single partner or placement so that one bad source cannot swamp the rest. And pay attention when a cheap channel suddenly scales; fraud scales instantly, and real audiences do not.

Why the fee structure matters here too

Every intermediary paid on volume has a reduced incentive to reject volume. A desk paid a flat fee, with rejection rate as a reported metric, is structurally aligned with catching fraud. A partner paid a percentage of spend is not. The controls above work best when the person applying them is not paid less for applying them.

lowob takeaway: Ad fraud is fake activity sold as performance, and it hides inside good-looking reports. Buy through inclusion lists with pre-bid verification, validate outcomes in your own systems, watch for numbers that are too clean, and use a partner who is not paid more when volume goes up.

Common questions

What is ad fraud?

Any scheme that generates fake advertising activity, such as impressions, clicks, installs, views or leads, so that someone is paid for attention that never happened. Most of it is paid for by advertisers whose reports show it as performance.

What are made-for-advertising (MFA) sites?

Pages that exist only to host ads, filled with cheap or scraped content and visited by traffic the owner bought from arbitrage sources. The visitors may be human, but the site has no audience anyone wanted to reach.

How can I protect my ad budget from fraud?

Buy through inclusion lists, require pre-bid verification on every programmatic buy and read the rejection report, validate every paid outcome in your own systems before paying, cap any single partner or placement, and watch for numbers that are too clean.

How much money is lost to ad fraud?

Estimates vary widely; industry bodies put global losses in the tens of billions of dollars a year. The share of a given advertiser's budget lost ranges from low single digits on well-controlled buys to a large fraction on unverified open-exchange buys.
